description: MMMU (Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning) is a benchmark of 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines (Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering) across 30 subjects and 183 subfields. It features 30 highly heterogeneous image types and interleaved text-image inputs, designed to evaluate expert-level perception and reasoning with domain-specific knowledge in large multimodal models.
name: MMMU
publisher: IN.AI Research, University of Waterloo, The Ohio State University
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students (including co-authors) specializing in the relevant academic majors across the 30 subjects covered by the benchmark. For human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students were selected to represent a wide range of experts in the corresponding 30 subjects (3 student experts per subject).
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human expert performance was measured on the validation set: the worst-performing expert achieved 76.2% accuracy, the median expert achieved 82.6%, and the best expert achieved 88.6%. Error analysis was conducted on 150 randomly sampled error instances from GPT-4V predictions, analyzed by expert annotators who identified root causes: 35% perceptual errors, 29% lack of knowledge, 26% reasoning errors, 4% textual understanding errors, 3% rejection to answer, 2% annotation errors, and 1% answer extraction errors.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators (over 50 university students specializing in the relevant majors) collected multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary. They were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoid data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution, and select questions without immediately available answers to avoid data contamination. A detailed annotation protocol is provided in Appendix H covering data collection, general guidelines, data format and structure, quality control and validation, handling ambiguities, ethical considerations, and data contamination considerations.
rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases. The focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. Annotators were advised to select questions without immediately available answers to mitigate data contamination concerns. The benchmark focuses on English-language questions from college-level curricula, which may not represent all global educational systems.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were manually collected by a team of over 50 college students (including co-authors) from various disciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, textbooks, and lecture materials. The collection process involved three stages: (1) selecting 30 subjects from six disciplines based on the principle that visual inputs should be commonly adopted; (2) recruiting university students specializing in these majors to collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary; (3) annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations and to select questions without immediately available answers to avoid data contamination.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Multimodal questions sourced from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, and online resources across 30 subjects and 6 disciplines. The raw collection resulted in approximately 13K questions from various sources before quality filtering.
rai:dataLimitations: MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI, as there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and "90th percentile of skilled adults," nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. A few subjects like law and linguistics were excluded because it was difficult to find enough relevant multimodal problems.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Two steps of data cleaning were performed: (1) lexical overlap and source URL similarity were employed to identify potential duplicate problems, which were then reviewed by authors to eliminate duplications; (2) problems were distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking, ensuring adherence to a standardized format. In a third stage, problems were categorized into four difficulty levels (very easy, easy, medium, hard), and approximately 10% classified as very easy were excluded from the benchmark.
rai:dataSocialImpact: MMMU is designed to monitor progress towards Expert AGI, which is defined as AI reaching "at least 90th percentile of skilled adults" in a broad range of tasks, potentially leading to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. The benchmark aims to provide a rigorous evaluation framework to track this progress and inform the research community.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating multimodal foundation models on expert-level, college-level multi-discipline tasks requiring domain-specific knowledge and deliberate reasoning. Monitoring progress towards Expert AGI. Stimulating the development of next-generation multimodal foundation models.

evidence.name: We introduce MMMU : a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning.
evidence.description: MMMU includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.

evidence.rai:dataBiases: MMMU , like any benchmark, has limitations despite its comprehensive nature. The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: We shall caution that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI, as per the definition, because there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and "90th percentile of skilled adults," nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We believe MMMU will stimulate the community to build next-generation multimodal foundation models towards expert artificial general intelligence.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Level 3, or Expert AGI, marks a critical milestone. It denotes an AI system that reaches "at least 90th percentile of skilled adults" in a broad range of tasks, thus starting to achieve "the substitution threshold for machine intelligence in lieu of human labor" for many industries, leading to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. Therefore, it is of both intellectual and societal importance to closely monitor the progress towards Expert AGI.
